# Introduction

In this Final Project, I am going to be using a dataset I found on Basketball Reference: [2025-26 NBA Player Stats: Totals](https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_2026_per_minute.html). The dataset features data from the 2025-2026 NBA season. Note that I am interested in predicting the number of minutes played and, since the website would only allow me to retrieve the top 500 players, I sorted by that variable before exporting the file.

A few notes to make on the data: First, I'm interested in what is more likely to earn a player playing time but I wanted to control for injuries so I created a column in the dataset which calculated my actual response variable: minutes played per game (`MPG`). Next, there were "missing" values in the 3 point percentage column (`3P%`) that reflected players that didn't attempt a 3 point shot (players who attempted at least one, but didn't make any, already had a value of `0` here). I added `0`'s in the places with missing cells, but I plan on using the `3P` column (made 3 point shots per 36 minutes played) so it should not make a difference in my analysis. Finally, I chose to export the data on a per 36 minutes basis, as cumulative total statistics will be heavily influenced by total minutes played.

There are obviously a lot of player statistics that get tracked but I am going to focus on the following predictor variables (again, all measured per 36 minutes played): three point shots made (`3P`), free throws made (`FT`), total rebounds (`TRB`), assists(`AST`), steals (`STL`), blocks (`BLK`), turnovers (`TOV`), personal fouls (`PF`), points (`PTS`), and position (`Pos`). Note that some of these are often combined in the analysis of NBA players (for instance, often a player's assist to turnover ratio or "stocks" [steals+blocks]). I thought combining these might deprive the model of some information (in exchange for having few variables, which I thought would be negligibly helpful), so I left them separate. 

# Reading in data, setting up libraries

Next, I will read in the data set and load the libraries I'll need for the modeling process. 

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# Load packages for data preparation, visualization, and modeling
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidymodels)
library(ranger)

#Create data tibble

min_played<-read_csv("../2025-26_NBA_Player_Stats_Per_36.csv")

min_played
```

Note that there there was very little pre-processing that needed to be done, and it was accomplished before reading the data in. 

Another important thing to mention is that we're dealing with numeric variables across the board here, with the exception of `Pos`, and all the columns are already formatted properly. 

# Splitting the data

Next up, I'll set a seed (one I'm partial to, $\approx \tau$), and split the data for modeling purposes (a 70/30 split, as requested). I choose to stratify the data by position, as the roles these players take on during the game can vary wildly. 

```{r}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

# Split data into training and test sets
mp_split <- initial_split(
  min_played, 
  prop = 0.7,
 )

# Isolate training and test sets

mp_train <- training(mp_split)
mp_test <- testing(mp_split)

# verify my 70/30 split
nrow(mp_train)/nrow(min_played)
nrow(mp_test)/nrow(min_played)
```
Doesn't get much better! 

# Creating Cross-Validation Folds

Next up is to create five cross-validation (CV) folds. For the models we'll be looking at, we'll fit using four of the folds and evaluate the resulting prediction on the fifth fold (all within the training dataset). These folds will be kept consistent between the models we use for fitting. 

```{r}
# Set seed
set.seed(6.28)

# Create five folds within training set
mp_folds <- vfold_cv(
  mp_train,
  v=5
)
```


# Fitting models

## Regression Tree Explanation

As mentioned above, we'll be using a variety of predictors in our model and we'll be predicting a numeric variable. So, we'll be using a regression tree here. With a regression tree, the predictor space is divided into regions and then, when making predictions, the observation is placed into one of these regions and (typically) the prediction is the average of the observed values in that region. 

To create these regions, every value of the predictor is used as a potential  splitting point and the squared error loss is calculated. Then, the minimum loss is found and the corresponding value for the prediction variable is used as the splitting point. This creates a branching effect (at each node) and then the process can be repeated down each branch, growing the tree. Of course, this process can lead to too many splits (too "large" a tree) and so these trees are often pruned back to avoid overfitting the data. 

### Setting up the Regression Tree Model

Before moving on, we should set up a recipe that we'll use for the regression tree and random forest models. This will be pretty straightforward since, with these models, we don't need to normalize the variables. We will, though, need the `Pos` variable set up as a dummy variable.  

```{r}
# Create recipe to be used with both models
mp_recipe <- recipe(MPG ~ `3P` + FT + TRB + AST + STL + BLK + TOV + PF+ PTS + Pos, data = mp_train)|>
  step_dummy(Pos)
mp_recipe
```


Next up, though, we will need to look at the hyperparameters we'd like to tune: 

```{r}
#Identify hyperparameters
rt_tune_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")
```

The next thing we'll need is a `tree_grid` for use in the tuning process. Because I have so many variables, I feel like I need to give the model room to make a lot of adjustments (e.g., fine tune the tree's depth). It feels like this might make the process take longer but, with what feels like a small sample size (`n`=500) and only 5 folds, it seems worth a shot. I reserve the right to set it back to 5, as we did in the homework, in which case you wouldn't be reading this anyway.

```{r}
rt_tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(),
                          tree_depth(),
                          levels = 10)
```

With that, we're ready for our workflow and CV resamples: 

```{r}
#set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

#Define workflow
rt_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(rt_tune_spec)|>
  add_recipe(mp_recipe)
  

#Set up resamples
rt_res <- rt_wf |>
  tune_grid(
    resamples = mp_folds,
    grid = rt_tree_grid
  )

#View results
rt_res
```

Let's see what we have here: 

```{r}
# Collect metrics
rt_res |> collect_metrics()
```

Let's pare this down a bit, to get a sense for how many models are close to the best: 

```{r}
# Show top 5 models, by chosen metric
rt_res |>
  show_best(metric = "rmse")
```

Looks like there's a tie at the top, but let's crown a winner anyway.

```{r}
#Pick the best tree
best_rt <- rt_res |>
  select_best(metric = "rmse")

best_rt
```

Now, to fit the model to the whole training dataset:

```{r}
#create final workflow
final_rt_wf <- rt_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(best_rt)

#Fit final model to training data
final_rt_fit <- final_rt_wf |>
  last_fit(mp_split)

final_rt_fit |> collect_metrics()
```

Nice! We have ourselves a fitted model (with an improvement in `rsme`)! 

## Random Forest Explanation

To start understanding random forests, we should start with with the idea behind bagged tree modelling. There, what happens is we would use either parametric or non-parametric bootstrap sampling to to fit a number of trees. As with all boostrapping, you begin by treating your sample as though it's the population, then sample *with replacement* to create a new sample of the same size as the original. In non-parametric, you do this directly from the original sample.In parametric you assume the sample comes from a particular distribution, estimate the parameters based on your sample, and then sample from that estimated distribution (still with a sample size matching that of the original sample).

Once you have some large number of bootstrap (re)samples, you would then fit a tree to each and finally, in the case of regression trees, we can average the predictions we get from these trees.

In the case of random forests, we do something similar but we don't use all the predictors at each step (split of the tree). Instead, we use a random subset of the predictors (the number used is a hyperparameter determined by tuning). 

The reason we do this is to to cut down on the correlation between models (which can be high when there's a particularly important explanatory variable) and cutting down on the correlation between models can lead to more of a reduction in variance when doing the averaging of predictions (and better predictions overall).

### Setting up the Random Forest Model

We'll actually be able to use a fair amount of the work from above here (including the split and CV folds from the regression tree model). One new thing that will help, though, is knowing how many processor cores we working with, to speed up the process. 

```{r}
#Find out how many cores
cores <- parallel::detectCores()
cores
```

Now, to create the model itself: 

```{r}
# Set up model
rf_mod <- 
  rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 1000) |> 
  set_engine("ranger", num.threads = cores, importance = "permutation") |> 
  set_mode("regression")
```

Nest, we'll create the workflow to train and tune the model.

```{r}
#set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

#create final workflow
rf_wf <- 
  workflow() |> 
  add_model(rf_mod) |> 
  add_recipe(mp_recipe)

#Set up resamples
rf_res <- 
  rf_wf |> 
  tune_grid(mp_folds,
            grid = 25,
            control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
            )

#View results
rf_res |> collect_metrics()
```

I see there's more variation in the `rmse`'s here, so let's start narrowing things down. 

```{r}
rf_res |>
  show_best(metric = "rmse")
```

These are looking better than the regression tree models we considered before, but let's fit it to the entire training set and see how things shake out. I'll pause here to note that our best model uses only half (5/10) of our predictor variables at each node (which surprised me). I would've expected that the variables I picked would have been different enough to warrant more of them being included. Having a small `min.n` of 3, though, means the trees run pretty deep. 

```{r}
#Pick the best model
best_rf <- rf_res |>
  select_best(metric = "rmse")

#create final workflow
final_rf_wf <- rf_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(best_rf)

#Fit final model to training data
final_rf_fit <- final_rf_wf |>
  last_fit(mp_split)

final_rf_fit |> collect_metrics()
```

As before, we got an improvement here! 

# Comparing the models

Now we're ready to compare the best regression tree and regression models. To start, let's look at the metrics we've seen before side-by-side.

```{r}
#set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

# Extract the best model metrics from each of the model families
best_rt_test <- final_rt_wf |>
  last_fit(mp_split, metrics = metric_set(rmse))

#set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

best_rf_test <- final_rf_wf |>
  last_fit(mp_split, metrics = metric_set(rmse))

# Combine the model metrics into one table, labeled for clarity
best_fits <- bind_rows(
  "Regression Tree" = collect_metrics(best_rt_test),
  "Random Forest" = collect_metrics(best_rf_test),
  .id = "model"
)
best_fits
```

## Regression Tree Summary

```{r}
rt_final_model <- extract_workflow(best_rt_test) 
rt_final_model |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.plot(roundint = FALSE)
```

It's really interesting to me that this tree is so simple, *and* only uses offensive statistics. I know that's what most fans focus on but I would have guess coaches (the people who decide on playing time) would have a more nuanced view which would've come through here.

## Random Forest Summary

For this summary, we'll look at the relative importance of each variable (since we don't have a single tree to analyze).

```{r}
rf_final_model <- best_rf_test |>
  extract_workflow() |>
  extract_fit_engine()

# Extract permutation variable importance
rf_importance <- tibble(
  term = names(rf_final_model$variable.importance),
  value = as.numeric(rf_final_model$variable.importance)
)

# Create the variable importance plot
rf_importance |>
  mutate(term = reorder(term, value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = term, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest Variable Importance",
    x = "Predictor",
    y = "Permutation Importance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

As before, this skews heavily to the offensive side of the ball. You have to get to the fifth variable (blocks) to get something anything related to defense. Of course, both blocks and steals are relatively rare (and therefore highly variable) events, so it's possible that there's simply too much noise there for that to be of much predictive value. Additionally, both blocks (accrued mostly by front court players) and steals (back court) are relatively position specific, which might have cut down on their importance. Going back to the beginning, perhaps including "stocks" would have been a better choice. 

## Fit the Best Overall Model

```{r}
# Rank models based on test RMSE
model_rankings <- best_fits |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  arrange(.estimate) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  select(rank, model, test_rmse = .estimate)

# Display results
knitr::kable(
  model_rankings,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Final Model Comparison Based on Test RMSE"
)
```

```{r}
# Declaration of the overall winner!
best_model_name <- model_rankings$model[1]

best_model_name
```

Finally, let's fit the winner to the whole data set, not just the training data.

```{r}
# Fit the selected model using the entire dataset
set.seed(6.28)

best_overall_fit <- fit(final_rf_wf, data = min_played)

# Display the final fitted model
best_overall_fit
```

Now that we have our model, fitted to the entire dataset, we could make predictions for new observations, like data from this year's season or years before last.
